Q1: Dispatch Call A (Maple St, chest pain, 7.8). It is the highest-scored waiting call, and per the principle the highest scorer wins the next unit even though nothing reaches 9.0. Holding the medic idle for a chest pain at 7.8 while waiting for a critical score would cost precious response time.

Q3: Dispatch Call A (1st St, person trapped, 8.9). Both are just below critical, and the decision still goes to the highest scorer — 8.9 beats 8.8. Call A involves a confirmed trapped occupant with smoke showing, so the ladder goes to 1st St without waiting.
Q4: Dispatch Call A (Hill Rd, diabetic emergency, 7.1). A 7.1 is a serious medical call needing a unit soon, and no threshold is needed to justify dispatching the highest scorer. Call B is only a standby at 5.5; the BLS unit goes to Hill Rd.
Q5: Dispatch Call A (River St, difficulty breathing, 8.1). The scores are nearly tied, but the principle is unambiguous: the highest urgency wins the next unit every time, regardless of threshold. 8.1 beats 8.0, and difficulty breathing is time-sensitive, so the medic goes to River St.
Q6: Dispatch Call A (Main St, vehicle fire, 6.8). The highest scorer takes the engine — 6.8 beats 6.5, and the mutual aid offer doesn't change which call our own unit answers. The neighboring jurisdiction's offer can cover Call B (brush fire near homes) as a follow-on, but our engine goes to Main St first.
Q7: Dispatch Call A (Park Ave, multi-vehicle accident, 7.5). It is the only call waiting, and the principle applies to every scenario: a scored call waiting with an available unit gets dispatched, never held for a threshold that isn't met. Command oversight at a multi-vehicle accident with injuries clearly warrants the battalion chief.
Q8: Dispatch Call A (Cedar Ln, stroke symptoms, 8.7). Stroke is time-critical with a closing treatment window, and 8.7 is the highest score in the queue — well above Call B's 7.3. Holding the medic for a 9.0 that hasn't arrived while a stroke window closes would be exactly the error the principle warns against.
Q9: Dispatch Call A (Summit Dr, gas leak, 5.9). With only one call waiting and an engine available, the decision is clear: a scored call gets the unit. The 9.0 threshold would trigger mutual aid and command notification, but nothing says a 5.9 waits idle — the engine goes to Summit Dr.
